solution: $\frac{1}{n^{3}}|k^{2}-9n^{2}|=\frac1n\left|\left(\frac kn\right)^{2}-9\right|$; $\frac kn$ runs over $(0,6]$ with step $\frac1n$
solution_full: Write $\dfrac{1}{n^{3}}\left|k^{2}-9n^{2}\right|=\dfrac1n\left|\left(\dfrac kn\right)^{2}-9\right|$. With $x_k=\frac kn$ and $\Delta x=\frac1n$, as $k$ runs from $1$ to $6n$, $x_k$ runs through $(0,6]$.
By the definition of the definite integral as a limit of a sum, the limit is $\int_0^{6}|x^{2}-9|\,dx$ ($|x^{2}-9|$ is continuous).
originality_note: New: a Riemann sum over [0,6] with a modulus that changes sign at k = 3n, so the sum cannot be done by one power-sum formula and the integral needs a split (way 5). Closest known: lim (1/n^3) sum k^2 = 1/3. Different because: the upper index 6n and the modulus change both the interval and the integrand.
blueprint_concepts: Definite integral as the limit of a sum

concept_use.Definite integral as the limit of a sum: The sum with k up to 6n and factor 1/n^3 is a Riemann sum for int_0^6 |x^2 - 9| dx; the modulus forces a split at x = 3 (k = 3n).

key_step: Recognise int_0^6 |x^2 - 9| dx and split at x = 3.
justification: Routine chain: identify the Riemann sum with upper limit 6n, then a modulus integral. Above 2021-P2-Q11 (L1) because of the extended range and modulus.
